title: Can an abstract class implement multiple interfaces and extend another abstract class at the same time?
shortTitle: Can an abstract class extend another class and implement interfaces?
keyPoints: Yes: an abstract class can extend one class (abstract or concrete) and implement multiple interfaces simultaneously
Being abstract, it can leave interface methods unimplemented for concrete subclasses to handle
This creates a layered hierarchy where each layer adds more specificity
A concrete (non-abstract) subclass at the bottom must implement all remaining abstract methods
This pattern is common in banking frameworks where a base entity is extended by domain-specific abstract classes
Each layer can provide partial implementations, reducing duplication across concrete subclasses

s1_definition.oneliner: Yes: an abstract class can extend one class (abstract or concrete) and implement multiple interfaces simultaneously. It can leave interface methods unimplemented for concrete subclasses. The concrete child at the bottom must implement all remaining abstract methods.
s1_definition.profdef:
An abstract class can simultaneously extend one other class and implement multiple interfaces.

- **Extends one class**: `abstract class InterestBearingAccount extends Account` inherits state and behavior from Account.
- **Implements multiple interfaces**: `implements Auditable, Taxable` declares capabilities.
- **Can leave methods unimplemented**: being abstract, it can defer interface method implementations to concrete subclasses.
- **Concrete subclass must finish**: a non-abstract class at the bottom of the chain must implement all remaining abstract methods from the parent chain and all unimplemented interface methods.
- **Creates layered hierarchy**: each layer adds more specificity. Account (base state) -> InterestBearingAccount (adds interest + declares Auditable) -> SavingsAccount (provides all implementations).
s1_definition.analogy: Think of it as a training manual at National Bank of India. Account (abstract class) is the master manual with common procedures (deposit, withdraw). InterestBearingAccount (abstract class) extends Account and adds interest-related procedures but leaves calculateInterest() for specific account types to define. It also implements Auditable and Taxable, declaring those capabilities. SavingsAccount (concrete class) extends InterestBearingAccount and provides all the missing pieces.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  LAYERED HIERARCHY
  ──────────────────────────────────────────

  Layer 1: Account (abstract)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ fields: accountId, balance       │
  │ concrete: deposit()              │
  │ abstract: getAccountType()       │
  └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
                 │ extends
  Layer 2: InterestBearingAccount (abstract)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ implements Auditable, Taxable    │
  │ fields: annualRate               │
  │ concrete: calculateMonthlyInterest()│
  │ abstract: getAccountType()       │
  │ abstract: generateAuditReport()  │
  │ abstract: calculateTax()         │
  └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
                 │ extends
  Layer 3: SavingsAccount (concrete)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
  │ implements ALL remaining methods │
  │ getAccountType() -> "SAVINGS"    │
  │ generateAuditReport() -> [...]   │
  │ calculateTax() -> 30% of interest│
  └─────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, an abstract class can simultaneously extend one other class and implement multiple interfaces. It does not need to implement all interface methods: being abstract, it can leave unimplemented methods for concrete subclasses. This creates a layered hierarchy where each layer adds more specificity: Account (base state) to InterestBearingAccount (adds interest and declares Auditable and Taxable) to SavingsAccount (provides all remaining implementations).

In Pankaj's banking system at National Bank of India, InterestBearingAccount extends Account (inheriting accountId, balance, deposit) and implements Auditable plus Taxable. It provides calculateMonthlyInterest() but leaves calculateTax() and getAccountType() abstract, so it must be declared abstract. SavingsAccount extends InterestBearingAccount and implements both remaining methods, making it concrete. FixedDepositAccount does the same with different tax rules.

Remember one sentence: an abstract class can extend one class and implement multiple interfaces, leaving unimplemented methods for concrete subclasses, which creates a layered hierarchy from general to specific.
